If you hand money to someone else's trading agent, you have to trust whoever runs it: not to take the money, and not to take more risk than they promised. Mandate turns that trust into contract terms. This is the live app on Monad testnet. Each card is a vault that an agent trades. Its limits, like maximum drawdown and leverage, are locked in the vault contract. The ring shows how much of the drawdown limit is still unused, and the status shows whether the agent may trade. In this video I play three roles: the operator who opens a vault, the allocator who funds it, and the agent that trades it.
Anyone can open a vault. Pick a preset, and one transaction deploys the vault, sets its terms and locks them before the first deposit. The operator cannot change them afterwards.
Now I am an allocator. I put a thousand test USDC into Tight Mandate. The money goes to the vault contract. The agent can trade it, but it can never withdraw it.
Now I am the agent. An order inside the terms passes the risk guard and executes. An order past the limit is refused before it reaches the venue, and the feed shows the contract's own error.

The market drops two percent, and this vault is now past its three percent drawdown limit. Anyone can act on that. Poke freezes the agent and pays the caller a small bounty. The agent's next order is refused, and the position is closed in public steps.
The allocator is never locked in. Withdrawals stay open through the freeze.

This vault refuses any price older than ten seconds. A mandate can only demand a price as fresh as its chain's blocks allow, and that is why Mandate is built on Monad. Every action here is a testnet transaction, like this poke on the explorer.

In this demo the venue and the USDC are mocks. The same guard also runs against Perpl's testnet exchange. Over five runs, a rule-based script had twenty orders filled and nine over-limit orders refused on chain.
